pack.description: Vocabulary of astronomy passages and talks: the solar system, stars, galaxies and observation.
pack.selection_note: Internal selection of terms that recur in introductory astronomy texts; this is not an official list and CEFR levels are author estimates.
pack.copyright_policy: Original content written for this app. No dictionary definition, ETS item or external word list was copied.

entries.definition: the curved path that a planet, moon or spacecraft follows around a larger body
entries.example_academic: The comet's orbit takes it far beyond the outermost planet.
entries.example_spoken: The station completes one orbit every ninety minutes.

entries.definition: a huge system of stars, gas and dust held together in space
entries.example_academic: Our galaxy contains several hundred billion stars.
entries.example_spoken: You can see another galaxy with binoculars on a clear night.

entries.definition: relating to the force that pulls objects with mass toward each other
entries.example_academic: The moon's gravitational pull is the main cause of ocean tides.
entries.example_spoken: Jupiter has a huge gravitational effect on nearby asteroids.

entries.definition: a rocky object, smaller than a planet, that travels around the sun
entries.example_academic: Most asteroids are found in a broad belt between Mars and Jupiter.
entries.example_spoken: An asteroid passed pretty close to Earth last week.

entries.definition: an object made of ice and dust that develops a bright tail when it comes near the sun
entries.example_academic: As the comet approaches the sun, its ice turns directly into gas.
entries.example_spoken: That comet only comes back every seventy-six years.

entries.definition: producing or reflecting a lot of light
entries.example_academic: The most luminous stars burn through their fuel in a few million years.
entries.example_spoken: The dial is luminous, so you can read it at night.

entries.definition: belonging to the sky or to space
entries.example_academic: Ancient calendars were based on the regular movement of celestial bodies.
entries.example_spoken: Sailors used celestial navigation before GPS existed.

entries.definition: an occasion when the moon or the Earth blocks the light of the sun or the moon for a short time
entries.example_academic: During a total solar eclipse, the outer atmosphere of the sun becomes visible.
entries.example_spoken: We drove six hours to watch the eclipse.

entries.definition: the action of turning around a central point or line
entries.example_academic: The planet's slow rotation means that a single day lasts several months.
entries.example_spoken: The Earth's rotation is why we have day and night.

entries.definition: the imaginary straight line around which an object turns
entries.example_academic: The tilt of the Earth's axis is responsible for the seasons.
entries.example_spoken: The globe spins on its axis, like this.

entries.definition: relating to the moon
entries.example_academic: Samples from the lunar surface are older than most rocks on Earth.
entries.example_spoken: There's a lunar eclipse tonight around eleven.

entries.definition: a piece of rock or metal from space that has landed on a planet
entries.example_academic: Chemical analysis of the meteorite revealed its age to be four billion years.
entries.example_spoken: The museum lets you touch a real meteorite.

entries.definition: relating to the whole universe and everything in space
entries.example_academic: Cosmic radiation poses a serious risk to astronauts on long missions.
entries.example_spoken: On a cosmic scale, a thousand years is nothing.

entries.definition: a group of stars that seem to form a pattern and has a name
entries.example_academic: Different cultures grouped the same stars into different constellations.
entries.example_spoken: Can you find that constellation near the horizon?

entries.definition: a building with large telescopes from which scientists study the sky
entries.example_academic: The observatory was built on a mountain to avoid atmospheric distortion.
entries.example_spoken: The campus observatory is open to the public on Fridays.

entries.definition: a spacecraft without people on board that is sent to collect information
entries.example_academic: The probe transmitted images of the planet's rings for over a decade.
entries.example_spoken: They lost contact with the probe just before landing.

entries.definition: a cloud of gas and dust in space, often where stars are forming
entries.example_academic: New stars are forming in the densest regions of the nebula.
entries.example_spoken: That fuzzy patch is a nebula, not a star.

entries.definition: the very bright explosion of a large star at the end of its life
entries.example_academic: A supernova scatters heavy elements that later become part of new planets.
entries.example_spoken: A supernova can outshine an entire galaxy for a few weeks.

entries.definition: a planet that travels around a star other than the sun
entries.example_academic: Thousands of exoplanets have been detected by the slight dimming of their stars.
entries.example_spoken: They found an exoplanet that might have liquid water.

entries.definition: existing or happening in the space between stars
entries.example_academic: Interstellar dust absorbs much of the visible light from the galactic center.
entries.example_spoken: Interstellar travel is still pure science fiction.

entries.definition: the gradual growth of an object as more material collects on it
entries.example_academic: Planets are thought to have formed through the accretion of dust and ice.
entries.example_spoken: The rings might be left over from accretion.

entries.definition: the study of light split into its colors in order to learn what something is made of
entries.example_academic: Spectroscopy allows astronomers to identify elements in a star's atmosphere.
entries.example_spoken: We used spectroscopy in lab to figure out what the gas was.

entries.definition: a change in the light from a distant object toward longer wavelengths, showing that it is moving away
entries.example_academic: The redshift of distant galaxies provides evidence that the universe is expanding.
entries.example_spoken: A bigger redshift means the galaxy is farther away.

entries.definition: a small, very dense star that turns quickly and sends out regular bursts of radio waves
entries.example_academic: The pulsar emits a beam that sweeps past Earth thirty times per second.
entries.example_spoken: At first they thought the pulsar signal came from aliens.

entries.definition: one of the two days in the year when day and night are the same length
entries.example_academic: At the equinox, the sun rises almost exactly in the east everywhere on Earth.
entries.example_spoken: The spring equinox is around March twentieth.

entries.definition: the scientific study of the origin and development of the universe
entries.example_academic: Modern cosmology rests on precise measurements of background radiation.
entries.example_spoken: She switched from particle physics to cosmology.

entries.definition: the total amount of light that a star or other object gives out
entries.example_academic: A star's luminosity depends on both its temperature and its size.
entries.example_spoken: You can estimate distance if you know the luminosity.

entries.definition: the boundary around a black hole beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape
entries.example_academic: Any signal emitted inside the event horizon can never reach an outside observer.
entries.example_spoken: Once you cross the event horizon, there's no coming back.

entries.definition: the region around a star where a planet could have liquid water on its surface
entries.example_academic: The planet lies near the inner edge of the habitable zone of its star.
entries.example_spoken: Earth is right in the middle of the habitable zone.
